A 68-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of hemoptysis and a 1-month history of mild cough, sputum production, and rhinorrhea. Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes mellitus, or vasculitis. On examination, vital signs were normal. Mild wheezing was auscultated bilaterally; neurologic and skin findings were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Initial microbiologic studies—including bacterial cultures, acid-fast bacillus smear and culture of sputum, blood cultures (bacterial and fungal), and respiratory viral serologies—were all negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodules and masses of various sizes in both lung fields, some with cavitation. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

A 39-year-old man with a history of treated tuberculosis presented with two weeks of fever, generalized weakness, vague abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, body aches, and moderate nasal bleeding. On examination, he had a 2×1 cm submandibular lymph node and hepatomegaly (7 cm below the costal margin), without gastrointestinal symptoms or skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed urea 18.8 mmol/L, creatinine 141 µmol/L, lipase 182 U/L, myoglobin 108 ng/mL, ferritin >40 000 µg/L, vitamin B12 <111 pmol/L, normal fibrinogen, and triglycerides. Viral serologies were negative. Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, WBC 1.7×10^3/µL, ANC 0.9×10^3/µL, platelets 2×10^3/µL. Head CT showed bilateral subdural hemorrhages without midline shift. Whole-body CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusion, extensive pulmonary consolidation, thrombosis of the celiac artery with splenic infarction, mild hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly with infarction. 

Initial peripheral smear showed very few atypical cells; a repeat smear revealed marked leukopenia and 13% abnormal blastoid cells of medium size with fine nuclear chromatin, unevenly distributed coarse basophilic granules, and occasional bilobed nuclei. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with 26% immature metachromatic blasts—cells with eccentric nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and coarse giant granules—as well as some agranular high N/C blasts and spindle-shaped cells. There was trilineage dysplasia with megaloblastic changes in granulocytes and erythroid precursors, dysplastic megakaryocytes, and frequent mitoses. Both histiocytes and the atypical cells demonstrated erythrophagocytosis.

A 56-year-old nulliparous woman presented 14 months after a supracervical laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for menorrhagia, pelvic pain, and large uterine leiomyomas. Her preoperative evaluation included a normal Pap smear; no chest radiograph or endometrial biopsy was obtained. At surgery, an 18–20-week–size uterus (1518 g) was removed via prolonged mechanical morcellation without a containment bag; superficial pelvic endometriosis was noted and cauterized. Final pathology on six uterine fragments demonstrated weakly proliferative endometrium without atypia, adenomyosis, and leiomyoma; the ovaries showed benign parenchyma and endosalpingiosis. 

On presentation, she reported left lower quadrant pain, persistent cough, and shortness of breath. Examination revealed a firm left lower quadrant abdominal mass and a fleshy lesion at the vaginal apex; the cervix was not visualized. PET–CT showed multiple hypermetabolic masses in the pelvis, abdomen, and chest. A core-needle biopsy of a 9 cm left pelvic mass revealed poorly differentiated epithelioid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for cytokeratin, vimentin, and CD138, and negative for SMA, EMA, ER, TLE1, HMB45, desmin, myogenin, CD117, BCL2, inhibin, MDN2, CD4, CA125, WT-1, CD45, calretinin, DOG-1, p16, CEA, CK20, HPV, and CD99. A vaginal biopsy showed grade 3 endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Pathology re-review of the hysterectomy and oophorectomy specimens showed no evidence of malignancy.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of bitemporal hemianopia and left labial numbness. On examination, he had visual impairment, bitemporal hemianopia, and right abducens nerve palsy. Laboratory studies showed: TSH 0.658 μU/mL, free thyroxine 0.41 ng/dL, growth hormone 0.62 ng/mL, LH < 0.2 mIU/mL, FSH < 1.0 mIU/mL, prolactin 19.7 ng/mL, cortisol 0.5 μg/dL, ACTH 16.4 pg/mL, testosterone < 5.0 ng/dL, and IGF-1 119 ng/mL (−0.73 SD), consistent with hypopituitarism. Dynamic pituitary stimulation tests confirmed gonadotropin, thyroid, and adrenal axis deficiencies and severe GH deficiency. Serum IgG4 was elevated at 319 mg/dL (normal 4.8–105), with a normal total IgG of 1284 mg/dL (IgG4/IgG ratio 0.25).  
Pituitary MRI demonstrated diffuse swelling of the pituitary body and stalk, a 7-mm poorly enhancing mass in the right anterior lobe, loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1-weighted images, and thickening of the sphenoid sinus mucosa. Chest CT revealed a nodular lesion in the left lung field, raising suspicion for systemic IgG4-related disease. No other organ involvement was identified on systemic imaging.  
Given the combination of hypopituitarism, elevated IgG4 levels, and imaging findings, the patient underwent endoscopic transnasal surgery of the pituitary gland for definitive diagnosis.

clinical_record:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Considered genetic or chromosomal cause of growth restriction

A 66-year-old woman with a history of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma presented with abdominal and pelvic pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, and laboratory studies, including a creatinine level of 0.81 mg dl–1, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right renal mass with areas of fat attenuation located in the upper pole, creating a defect in the renal parenchyma. The lesion contained visible vessels extending into the renal cortex, a finding known as a “renal parenchymal vascular pedicle.” Additionally, there was a fatty tumor thrombus within the right renal vein extending to its confluence with the inferior vena cava. No other masses or enlarged lymph nodes were identified.

A 48-year-old man with a 12-year history of perianal fistula presented with recent mucinous discharge, pain, and perianal induration. One year earlier, he had undergone incision and drainage of a recurrent perianal abscess. 

On examination, there were two indurated, ulcerative lesions each 7 cm in diameter and three external fistula openings around the anus; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Upper endoscopy was unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed the internal fistula opening at the right side of the dentate line, with otherwise normal mucosa in the rectum and colon on digital and endoscopic examination.

Abdominopelvic CT and MRI demonstrated a well-defined mass at the level of the anorectal junction extending into the right ischiorectal fossa, with enlarged pelvic lymph nodes but no inguinal nodal or distant metastases.

Histological examination of a biopsy specimen from the indurated area revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma. A serum carcinoembryonic antigen level was within the normal range.

His medications included lisinopril, atorvastatin, albuterol, and ibuprofen for rheumatoid arthritis. The patient had discontinued etanercept six months before presentation. He presented to the emergency department two weeks after seeing his primary care provider for a persistent periorbital, chest, and upper extremity rash. There was a heliotrope rash and erythematous lip swelling. He had weakness to resistance in all extremities and a muffled voice without tongue swelling. An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

An 8-year-old girl weighing 44.5 kg with no significant medical history presented with a 1-week history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination revealed notable abdominal distension without guarding or rebound. Initial abdominal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm mixed solid and cystic mass occupying the right hepatic lobe with compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). By hospital day 7, worsening abdominal distension and concern for abdominal compartment syndrome prompted percutaneous biopsy of the mass and placement of a drain. Over the next several days, persistent sanguineous output from the drain led to anemia and concern for hemorrhage. Additional findings included a right calyceal calculus with mild pelvicalyceal dilatation, a simple right renal cyst, no pelvic lymphadenopathy, and left hydrosalpinx.

On imaging, possibilities such as endometriosis, a mucosal neoplastic lesion, or a granulomatous lesion of the urinary bladder were considered.

An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. One month after surgery, follow-up MRI confirmed persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, skull base, and pterygoid fossa. A consultation with an infectious diseases specialist was sought.
